claim: Nineteen subjects participated in the study after four subjects were excluded due to excessive movements in the scanner.
source: Twenty-three healthy volunteers participated in the study. All participants were right-handed and neurologically healthy, with normal or corrected-to-normal vision. The experiment was approved by the Institutional Review Board of the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke. All subjects provided written informed consent. Four subjects were excluded due to excessive movements in the scanner, leaving 19 subjects for the analyses reported herein (age range = 19–32; mean age = 24.6; 11 females).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript's Methods section with specific numbers and exclusion criteria.

claim: Disambiguation by viewing the gray-scale images significantly increased recognition rate for Mooney images from 43 ± 12% pre-disambiguation to 86 ± 1% post-disambiguation.
source: Disambiguation by viewing the gray-scale images had a substantial effect on participants' subjective recognition responses, with significantly higher rate of recognition for Mooney images presented post-disambiguation (86 ± 1%; mean ± s.d. across subjects) compared to the same images presented before disambiguation (43 ± 12%; t1,18 = 18.6, p=3.4e-13, Cohen's d = 4.2; Figure 1B, left).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis (t-test) with specific p-value and effect size, and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Mooney images were correctly identified significantly more often after disambiguation (86 ± 0.8%) than before (34 ± 12%).
source: A similar pattern of results was observed using the verbal identification responses. Mooney images were correctly identified significantly more often after disambiguation (86 ± 0.8%) than before (34 ± 12%; t1,18 = 25.3, p=1.7e-15, Cohen's d = 5.8; Figure 1B, right).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis with specific values and referenced in Figure 1B.

claim: Disambiguation had a dramatic effect on recognition rate (F1,18 = 345.6, p=3.4e-13, η2p =.95).
source: A two-way ANOVA on recognition rate with presentation number (Bastos et al., 2012; Mumford, 1992; Yuille and Kersten, 2006; Albright, 2012; Summerfield and de Lange, 2014; Trapp and Bar, 2015) and disambiguation stage (pre- vs. post-) as factors revealed that disambiguation had a dramatic effect on recognition rate (F1,18 = 345.6, p=3.4e-13, η2p =.95, while repetition also improved recognition (F5,90 = 8.1, p=0.002, η2p = 0.3) (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by two-way ANOVA statistical test with specific F-statistic, p-value, and effect size.

claim: Repetition improved recognition (F5,90 = 8.1, p=0.002, η2p = 0.3).
source: A two-way ANOVA on recognition rate with presentation number (Bastos et al., 2012; Mumford, 1992; Yuille and Kersten, 2006; Albright, 2012; Summerfield and de Lange, 2014; Trapp and Bar, 2015) and disambiguation stage (pre- vs. post-) as factors revealed that disambiguation had a dramatic effect on recognition rate (F1,18 = 345.6, p=3.4e-13, η2p =.95, while repetition also improved recognition (F5,90 = 8.1, p=0.002, η2p = 0.3) (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by two-way ANOVA statistical test with specific F-statistic, p-value, and effect size.

claim: The interaction between disambiguation stage and presentation number was significant (F5,90 = 7.5, p=0.001, η2p = 0.29).
source: The interaction between these two factors was significant (F5,90 = 7.5, p=0.001, η2p = 0.29).
evidence: Supported by statistical test with specific values.

claim: The repetition effect was driven by pre-disambiguation images, with recognition rate increasing gradually across presentations before disambiguation (p<0.05), but not after disambiguation (p=1).
source: A post-hoc analysis (Bonferroni-corrected) suggested that the repetition effect was driven by pre-disambiguation images, with recognition rate increasing gradually across presentations before disambiguation (p<0.05), but not after disambiguation (p=1).
evidence: Supported by post-hoc statistical analysis with Bonferroni correction.

claim: For pre-disambiguation images, the recognition rate was significantly higher in the sixth presentation (47 ± 14%) compared to the first presentation (36 ± 13%; paired t-test across subjects, t1,18 = 4.2, p=0.007, Cohen's d = 0.97).
source: For instance, for pre-disambiguation images, the recognition rate was significantly higher in the sixth presentation (47 ± 14%, mean ± s.d. across subjects) compared to the first presentation (36 ± 13%; paired t-test across subjects, t1,18 = 4.2, p=0.007, Cohen's d = 0.97), suggesting that participants did not stop attending after being unable to recognize Mooney images at first, and actively tried to recognize these in subsequent presentations.
evidence: Supported by paired t-test with specific statistics.

claim: Disambiguated Mooney images elicited significantly higher activity in regions of the DMN, including the posterior cingulate cortex (PCC), lateral parietal cortices (Par Lat), and the medial prefrontal cortex (MPFC) than the same images presented pre-disambiguation (p<0.05, FWE-corrected).
source: First, consistent with earlier studies (Dolan et al., 1997; Gorlin et al., 2012), we found that disambiguated Mooney images elicited significantly higher activity in regions of the DMN, including the posterior cingulate cortex (PCC), lateral parietal cortices (Par Lat), and the medial prefrontal cortex (MPFC) than the same images presented pre-disambiguation (Figure 2A, p<0.05, FWE-corrected; results using verbal identification responses are similar and presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by GLM analysis with FWE correction and shown in Figure 2A, with citation to earlier studies.

claim: The increased activity in DMN regions after disambiguation resulted from a reduced deactivation in the post-disambiguation period (p<0.05, FWE-corrected).
source: A more detailed analysis revealed that this effect resulted from a reduced deactivation in the post-disambiguation period (Figure 2B, p<0.05, FWE-corrected).
evidence: Supported by detailed GLM analysis with FWE correction and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Information about the status of a Mooney image was contained in the voxel-wise activity pattern in an extensive set of brain regions (p<0.01, corrected by cluster-based permutation test), comprising mainly the FPN, but also including the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), bilateral anterior insulae, fusiform gyri (FG), and components of the DMN.
source: Using a searchlight decoding analysis across the whole brain, we found that information about the status of a Mooney image was contained in the voxel-wise activity pattern in an extensive set of brain regions (Figure 2C, p<0.01, corrected by cluster-based permutation test; results using verbal identification responses are similar and presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 2), comprising mainly the FPN (Dosenbach et al., 2008), but also including the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), bilateral anterior insulae, fusiform gyri (FG), and components of the DMN.
evidence: Supported by searchlight decoding analysis with cluster-based permutation test correction and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Disambiguation increased representational dissimilarity between individual images in all ROIs investigated, including FPN and DMN.
source: Strikingly, disambiguation increased representational dissimilarity between individual images in all ROIs investigated, including FPN and DMN. This can be seen from the gradient of color difference between the Pre-Pre square and the Post-Post square in the RDM (Figures 3B and 4A, which include mid-line and right hemisphere ROIs; see Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1 for similar results from the left hemisphere ROIs, and Figure 3—figure supplement 2 for similar results from V4).
evidence: Supported by RSA analysis shown in multiple figures (3B, 4A, and supplements).

claim: Representational dissimilarity between individual Mooney images significantly increased after disambiguation in all ROIs investigated across both hemispheres, except the left V2 and left V4 (all p<0.05, FDR-corrected).
source: Representational dissimilarity between individual Mooney images significantly increased after disambiguation in all ROIs investigated across both hemispheres, except the left V2 and left V4 (Figure 3D and 4C, cyan brackets, all p<0.05, FDR-corrected, assessed by paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test across subjects; and see panel C of Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 2), suggesting that Mooney images are represented more distinctly after disambiguation throughout the cortical hierarchy.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis (Wilcoxon signed-rank test) with FDR correction and shown in multiple figures.

claim: Representational dissimilarity between different images within each condition gradually increased from early visual areas to category-selective visual regions, to FPN and DMN.
source: In addition, representational dissimilarity between different images within each condition (shown as the height of bars in Figure 3D and 4C) gradually increased from early visual areas to category-selective visual regions, to FPN and DMN.
evidence: Observed pattern in the data shown in Figures 3D and 4C.

claim: For grayscale images, category information is significant in category-selective visual regions (bilateral LOC and FG), as well as parietal regions of the FPN and DMN (all p<0.05, FDR-corrected).
source: This analysis (Figure 4—figure supplement 3) showed that for grayscale images, category information is significant in category-selective visual regions (bilateral LOC and FG), as well as parietal regions of the FPN and DMN (including bilateral parietal cortices of FPN, right Par Lat and PCC of DMN) (all p<0.05, FDR-corrected).
evidence: Supported by category information analysis with FDR correction and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: For pre-disambiguation Mooney images, no significant category information was found in any ROI.
source: For pre-disambiguation Mooney images, no significant category information was found in any ROI; however, for post-disambiguation Mooney images, significant category information was present in the right LOC and bilateral FG only (p<0.05, FDR-corrected).
evidence: Supported by category information analysis with FDR correction.

claim: For post-disambiguation Mooney images, significant category information was present in the right LOC and bilateral FG only (p<0.05, FDR-corrected).
source: For pre-disambiguation Mooney images, no significant category information was found in any ROI; however, for post-disambiguation Mooney images, significant category information was present in the right LOC and bilateral FG only (p<0.05, FDR-corrected).
evidence: Supported by category information analysis with FDR correction.

claim: In all ROIs investigated across both hemispheres, from early and category-selective visual areas to FPN and DMN regions, the representational similarity between a post-disambiguation Mooney image and its matching gray-scale image is greater than that between a pre-disambiguation Mooney image and its matching gray-scale image (all p<0.05, FDR-corrected).
source: In all ROIs investigated across both hemispheres, from early and category-selective visual areas to FPN and DMN regions, the representational similarity between a post-disambiguation Mooney image and its matching gray-scale image is greater than that between a pre-disambiguation Mooney image and its matching gray-scale image (Figure 3E and 4D, red brackets; all p<0.05, FDR-corrected, Wilcoxon signed-rank tests across subjects; and see panel D of Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis (Wilcoxon signed-rank test) with FDR correction and shown in multiple figures.

claim: In all ROIs except V1, post-disambiguation Mooney images were represented more similarly to their grayscale counterparts than to the same Mooney images shown before disambiguation (all p<0.05, FDR-corrected).
source: Interestingly, in all ROIs except V1, post-disambiguation Mooney images were represented more similarly to their grayscale counterparts than to the same Mooney images shown before disambiguation (Figure 3E and 4D, green brackets; all p<0.05, FDR-corrected, Wilcoxon signed-rank tests; and see panel D of Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis (Wilcoxon signed-rank test) with FDR correction and shown in multiple figures.

claim: A similar trend is present in V1, albeit not significant (right V1: p=0.06; left V1: p=0.07).
source: A similar trend is present in V1, albeit not significant (right V1: p=0.06; left V1: p=0.07).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis with specific p-values.

claim: A repeated-measures ANOVA revealed a significant condition (pre- vs. post-disambiguation) × set ('disambiguation' vs. 'repetition') interaction for higher between-image dissimilarity for post- than pre-disambiguation images (F1,14 = 4.6, p=0.05).
source: Using a repeated-measures ANOVA, we found a significant condition (pre- vs. post-disambiguation) × set ('disambiguation' vs. 'repetition') interaction for all neural effects of interest: higher between-image dissimilarity for post- than pre-disambiguation images (cyan brackets in Figure 3 and 4, F1,14 = 4.6, p=0.05); higher within-image similarity for post-Gray than pre-Gray comparison (red brackets, F1,14 =14.9, p=0.002); higher within-image similarity for post-Gray than pre-post comparison (green brackets; F1,14 = 6.3, p=0.02).
evidence: Supported by repeated-measures ANOVA with specific F-statistics and p-values.

claim: A repeated-measures ANOVA revealed a significant condition × set interaction for higher within-image similarity for post-Gray than pre-Gray comparison (F1,14 =14.9, p=0.002).
source: Using a repeated-measures ANOVA, we found a significant condition (pre- vs. post-disambiguation) × set ('disambiguation' vs. 'repetition') interaction for all neural effects of interest: higher between-image dissimilarity for post- than pre-disambiguation images (cyan brackets in Figure 3 and 4, F1,14 = 4.6, p=0.05); higher within-image similarity for post-Gray than pre-Gray comparison (red brackets, F1,14 =14.9, p=0.002); higher within-image similarity for post-Gray than pre-post comparison (green brackets; F1,14 = 6.3, p=0.02).
evidence: Supported by repeated-measures ANOVA with specific F-statistics and p-values.

claim: A repeated-measures ANOVA revealed a significant condition × set interaction for higher within-image similarity for post-Gray than pre-post comparison (F1,14 = 6.3, p=0.02).
source: Using a repeated-measures ANOVA, we found a significant condition (pre- vs. post-disambiguation) × set ('disambiguation' vs. 'repetition') interaction for all neural effects of interest: higher between-image dissimilarity for post- than pre-disambiguation images (cyan brackets in Figure 3 and 4, F1,14 = 4.6, p=0.05); higher within-image similarity for post-Gray than pre-Gray comparison (red brackets, F1,14 =14.9, p=0.002); higher within-image similarity for post-Gray than pre-post comparison (green brackets; F1,14 = 6.3, p=0.02).
evidence: Supported by repeated-measures ANOVA with specific F-statistics and p-values.

claim: The 2-D MDS solution of the second-order RDM reveals an organization in accordance with known anatomical and functional networks (r2 = 0.92, stress = 0.06).
source: The 2-D MDS solution of the second-order RDM reveals an organization in accordance with known anatomical and functional networks (Figure 5C; r2 = 0.92, stress = 0.06, that is, the 2-D MDS solution explains 92% of variance in the high-dimensional RDM and has a high goodness-of-fit).
evidence: Supported by MDS analysis with specific goodness-of-fit metrics and shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Regions are located along a gradient consistent with the visual hierarchy (Dimension 1), which ranges from V1 – V4, to LOC and FG, then frontoparietal regions.
source: Moreover, regions are located along a gradient consistent with the visual hierarchy (Dimension 1), which ranges from V1 – V4, to LOC and FG, then frontoparietal regions.
evidence: Observed pattern in the MDS analysis described in the text.

claim: The hierarchy of neural representation format mirrors a principal gradient of macroscale cortical organization recently found based on resting-state functional connectivity and cortical anatomy, with sensory areas and DMN situated at the two extremes of the gradient, and FPN being intermediate.
source: In addition, this hierarchy mirrors a principal gradient of macroscale cortical organization recently found based on resting-state functional connectivity and cortical anatomy, with sensory areas and DMN situated at the two extremes of the gradient, and FPN being intermediate (Margulies et al., 2016).
evidence: Comparison with previous findings from Margulies et al., 2016.

claim: The 2-D MDS solutions for each within-condition second-order RDM all have high goodness-of-fit (pre-disambiguation: r2 = 0.91, stress = 0.07; Gray-scale: r2 = 0.93, stress = 0.06; post-disambiguation: r2 = 0.90, stress = 0.09).
source: The 2-D MDS solutions for each within-condition second-order RDM are shown in Figure 5D, bottom, and all have high goodness-of-fit (pre-disambiguation: r2 = 0.91, stress = 0.07; Gray-scale: r2 = 0.93, stress = 0.06; post-disambiguation: r2 = 0.90, stress = 0.09).
evidence: Supported by MDS analysis with specific goodness-of-fit metrics for each condition.

claim: There is a stable overall hierarchy of representation format across ROIs, despite changes in neural representation within each ROI due to disambiguation.
source: Comparing the MDS solutions across perceptual conditions suggested that, indeed, there is a stable overall hierarchy of representation format across ROIs, despite changes in neural representation within each ROI due to disambiguation (as shown in Figure 3 and 4).
evidence: Inference from comparing MDS solutions across conditions shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Following disambiguation, frontal regions of the FPN rise higher up in the hierarchy such that the principal gradient (Dimension 1) separates frontal from parietal regions.
source: An interesting, qualitative variation on this theme is that frontal regions of the FPN rise higher up in the hierarchy after disambiguation, such that the principal gradient (Dimension 1) separates frontal from parietal regions (Figure 5D, right panel), instead of DMN from FPN (Figure 5D, left and middle).
evidence: Observed pattern in the MDS plots shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Dimensionality of neural representational space is relatively low in early visual areas and LOC, but substantially higher in FG, FPN and DMN regions.
source: The group-averaged dimensionality for each ROI is shown in Figure 6A–C. A large-scale gradient can be seen in every perceptual condition: Dimensionality of neural representational space is relatively low in early visual areas and LOC, but substantially higher in FG, FPN and DMN regions.
evidence: Observed pattern in the dimensionality analysis shown in Figure 6A-C.

claim: Both the network (p=3.1e-16) and the condition (p=2e-6) factors significantly impacted dimensionality, while the interaction was not significant (p=0.29).
source: Both main effects were highly significant (network: F56,4 = 41.96, p=3.1e-16, η2p = 0.75; condition: F28,2 = 22.27, p=2e-6, η2p = 0.61), while the interaction was not significant (p=0.29, η2p = 0.08).
evidence: Supported by two-way repeated-measures ANOVA with specific F-statistics and p-values.

claim: Compared to early visual areas (2.9 ± 0.3), dimensionality was significantly higher in FG (4.6 ± 0.9), FPN (4.6 ± 1) and DMN (4.3 ± 0.7; all ps < 0.001), but not LOC (3.1 ± 0.6; p>0.3).
source: Post-hoc tests (Bonferroni-corrected) revealed that compared to early visual areas (2.9 ± 0.3; mean ±s.d. across subjects), dimensionality was significantly higher in FG (4.6 ± 0.9), FPN (4.6 ± 1) and DMN (4.3 ± 0.7; all ps < 0.001), but not LOC (3.1 ± 0.6; p>0.3).
evidence: Supported by post-hoc tests with Bonferroni correction and specific p-values.

claim: Dimensionality did not differ significantly between FG and FPN or DMN (all ps > 0.08).
source: On the other hand, dimensionality did not differ significantly between FG and FPN or DMN (all ps > 0.08).
evidence: Supported by post-hoc statistical comparisons.

claim: Dimensionality was significantly higher for both post-disambiguation Mooney images (4 ± 1.1) and grayscale images (4.1 ± 1.1) than pre-disambiguation Mooney images (3.7 ± 0.7; both p<0.001).
source: Comparing across perceptual conditions, dimensionality was significantly higher for both post-disambiguation Mooney images (4 ± 1.1) and grayscale images (4.1 ± 1.1) than pre-disambiguation Mooney images (3.7 ± 0.7; both p<0.001), while the difference between post-disambiguation Mooney images and grayscale images was not significant (p>0.16).
evidence: Supported by post-hoc statistical comparisons with specific p-values.

claim: The difference in dimensionality between post-disambiguation Mooney images and grayscale images was not significant (p>0.16).
source: Comparing across perceptual conditions, dimensionality was significantly higher for both post-disambiguation Mooney images (4 ± 1.1) and grayscale images (4.1 ± 1.1) than pre-disambiguation Mooney images (3.7 ± 0.7; both p<0.001), while the difference between post-disambiguation Mooney images and grayscale images was not significant (p>0.16).
evidence: Supported by post-hoc statistical comparison with specific p-value.

claim: The neural code of Mooney images was significantly preserved following disambiguation in early visual areas, LOC, FG, and the FPN (all p<0.05, FDR-corrected).
source: This analysis revealed a large-scale trend of decreasing PI towards higher-order brain regions (Figure 7B). The neural code of Mooney images was significantly preserved following disambiguation in early visual areas, LOC, FG, and the FPN (all p<0.05, FDR-corrected, one-sample t-tests across subjects).
evidence: Supported by preservation index analysis with FDR correction and shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The preservation index did not differ significantly from zero in DMN regions (all p>0.05).
source: However, the preservation index did not differ significantly from zero in DMN regions (all p>0.05).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis with specific p-values.

claim: A repeated-measures ANOVA revealed a significant effect of Network on preservation index (F56,4 = 41.86, p=3.27e-16, η2p = 0.75).
source: To assess differences in PI across networks, we performed a repeated-measures ANOVA with network (Visual, LOC, FG, FPN, and DMN) being the independent factor and PI being the dependent variable. This analysis revealed a significant effect of Network (F56,4 = 41.86, p=3.27e-16, η2p = 0.75).
evidence: Supported by repeated-measures ANOVA with specific F-statistic and p-value.

claim: Post-hoc pairwise comparisons between individual networks were all significant (all ps < 0.015, Bonferroni corrected), except between Visual and LOC (p=0.81), or between FPN and DMN (p=1).
source: Post-hoc pairwise comparisons between individual networks were all significant (all ps < 0.015, Bonferroni corrected), except between Visual and LOC (p=0.81), or between FPN and DMN (p=1).
evidence: Supported by post-hoc pairwise comparisons with Bonferroni correction.

claim: An additional repeated-measures ANOVA with three levels for the Network factor (parietal regions of the FPN, frontal regions of the FPN, and the DMN) yielded a significant effect of Network (F36,2 = 6.86, p=0.003, η2p = 0.28).
source: To statistically assess this difference, we performed an additional repeated-measures ANOVA with only three levels for the Network factor (parietal regions of the FPN, frontal regions of the FPN, and the DMN). This analysis yielded again a significant effect of Network (F36,2 = 6.86, p=0.003, η2p = 0.28).
evidence: Supported by repeated-measures ANOVA with specific F-statistic and p-value.

claim: PI was higher in FPN-parietal regions than FPN-frontal regions (p=0.001) or the DMN (p=0.02).
source: Post-hoc comparisons (Bonferroni-corrected) revealed that PI was higher in FPN-parietal regions than FPN-frontal regions (p=0.001) or the DMN (p=0.02).
evidence: Supported by post-hoc comparisons with Bonferroni correction.

claim: The difference in PI between FPN-frontal regions and the DMN was not significant (p=1).
source: In contrast, the difference between FPN-frontal regions and the DMN was not significant (p=1).
evidence: Supported by post-hoc comparison with specific p-value.

claim: Prior knowledge shapes perceptual processing across the human brain, particularly in the frontoparietal (FPN) and default-mode (DMN) networks.
source: How prior knowledge shapes perceptual processing across the human brain, particularly in the frontoparietal (FPN) and default-mode (DMN) networks, remains unknown.
evidence: This is the research question being addressed, stated in the abstract.

claim: Prior knowledge significantly impacted neural representations in the FPN and DMN, rendering responses to individual visual images more distinct from each other, and more similar to the image-specific prior.
source: We observed that prior knowledge significantly impacted neural representations in the FPN and DMN, rendering responses to individual visual images more distinct from each other, and more similar to the image-specific prior.
evidence: Summary of main findings stated in the abstract.

claim: Neural representations were structured in a hierarchy that remained stable across perceptual conditions, with early visual areas and DMN anchored at the two extremes.
source: In addition, neural representations were structured in a hierarchy that remained stable across perceptual conditions, with early visual areas and DMN anchored at the two extremes.
evidence: Summary of main findings stated in the abstract.

claim: Dimensionality of the neural representational space increased along the hierarchy.
source: Two large-scale cortical gradients occur along this hierarchy: first, dimensionality of the neural representational space increased along the hierarchy; second, prior's impact on neural representations was greater in higher-order areas.
evidence: Summary of main findings stated in the abstract.

claim: Prior's impact on neural representations was greater in higher-order areas.
source: Two large-scale cortical gradients occur along this hierarchy: first, dimensionality of the neural representational space increased along the hierarchy; second, prior's impact on neural representations was greater in higher-order areas.
evidence: Summary of main findings stated in the abstract.

claim: Perception arises as a consequence of a continuous interaction between incoming sensory input and internal priors.
source: Although it is well established that perception arises as a consequence of a continuous interaction between incoming sensory input and internal priors (Bastos et al., 2012; Mumford, 1992; Yuille and Kersten, 2006; Albright, 2012; Summerfield and de Lange, 2014; Trapp and Bar, 2015), the neural mechanisms underlying this process remain unclear.
evidence: Established scientific consensus cited from multiple sources.

claim: Extensive research has focused on how prior experience and knowledge shape neural processing in early sensory areas.
source: In particular, while extensive research has focused on how prior experience and knowledge shape neural processing in early sensory areas (e.g., [Kok et al., 2012; Schlack and Albright, 2007; Alink et al., 2010; Hsieh et al., 2010]), whether higher-order frontoparietal regions contain content-specific neural representations that are involved in prior-guided perceptual processing remains unknown.
evidence: Summary of existing research with citations.

claim: Whether higher-order frontoparietal regions contain content-specific neural representations that are involved in prior-guided perceptual processing remains unknown.
source: In particular, while extensive research has focused on how prior experience and knowledge shape neural processing in early sensory areas (e.g., [Kok et al., 2012; Schlack and Albright, 2007; Alink et al., 2010; Hsieh et al., 2010]), whether higher-order frontoparietal regions contain content-specific neural representations that are involved in prior-guided perceptual processing remains unknown.
evidence: Statement of knowledge gap in the field.

claim: Classic theories suggest that the DMN is involved in internally oriented processes.
source: Classic theories suggest that the DMN is involved in internally oriented processes (Buckner et al., 2008), such as self-related processing (Kelley et al., 2002), spontaneous/task irrelevant thought (Mason et al., 2007; Christoff et al., 2009), episodic and semantic memory (Shapira-Lichter et al., 2013; Binder et al., 2009; Sestieri et al., 2011).
evidence: Summary of classic theories with citations.

claim: Recent studies show DMN activation in externally oriented tasks, including executive control and working memory tasks.
source: This idea is challenged by recent studies showing DMN activation in externally oriented tasks, including executive control and working memory tasks (Crittenden et al., 2015; Konishi et al., 2015; Vatansever et al., 2015).
evidence: Summary of recent findings with citations.

claim: The DMN, being positioned farthest away from uni-modal sensory and motor areas in both functional connectivity and anatomical space, allows online information processing to be guided by stored representations.
source: These results have inspired a recent framework suggesting that the DMN, being positioned farthest away from uni-modal sensory and motor areas in both functional connectivity and anatomical space, allows online information processing to be guided by stored representations (Margulies et al., 2016).
evidence: Recent theoretical framework with citation.

claim: Evidence for content-specific activity in the DMN during externally-oriented tasks is still lacking.
source: However, to date evidence for content-specific activity in the DMN during externally-oriented tasks is still lacking, which would be crucial for establishing this network's role in specific computations linking online processing with stored representations.
evidence: Statement of knowledge gap in the field.

claim: The role of DMN in prior-guided visual perception remains controversial.
source: In particular, the role of DMN in prior-guided visual perception remains controversial (Dolan et al., 1997; Gorlin et al., 2012).
evidence: Statement of controversy with citations.

claim: One framework suggests that the FPN only encodes task/response-relevant information.
source: One framework suggests that this network only encodes task/response-relevant information (Erez and Duncan, 2015; Bracci et al., 2017), such as learnt arbitrary categories of visual objects that are relevant to performance (Freedman et al., 2001) or the distinction between a target and a non-target (Erez and Duncan, 2015).
evidence: Summary of one theoretical framework with citations.

claim: Neural activity reflecting perceptual content has been observed in both the lateral prefrontal cortex (LPFC) and posterior-parietal cortex (PPC) components of the FPN.
source: On the other hand, neural activity reflecting perceptual content has been observed in both the lateral prefrontal cortex (LPFC)(Wang et al., 2013; Panagiotaropoulos et al., 2012; Mendoza-Halliday and Martinez-Trujillo, 2017) and posterior-parietal cortex (PPC)(Jeong and Xu, 2016; Konen and Kastner, 2008; Freud et al., 2016) components of this network, even when task demand is held constant or was irrelevant to the perceptual content (e.g., [Panagiotaropoulos et al., 2012; Mendoza-Halliday and Martinez-Trujillo, 2017; Konen and Kastner, 2008]).
evidence: Summary of existing findings with citations.

claim: Whether the LPFC contributes to visual perceptual processing is a heavily debated topic.
source: Currently, whether the LPFC contributes to visual perceptual processing is a heavily debated topic (Dehaene et al., 2017; Koch et al., 2016).
evidence: Statement of ongoing debate with citations.

claim: In anatomical and functional connectivity space, the FPN is situated in between the DMN and sensory areas.
source: Inspired by the observation that in anatomical and functional connectivity space, the FPN is situated in between the DMN and sensory areas (Margulies et al., 2016), we reasoned that the FPN may exhibit an intermediate pattern of effects compared to the DMN and sensory areas during prior-guided perceptual processing.
evidence: Observation from previous study with citation.

claim: Mooney images are black-and-white degraded images that are difficult to recognize at first.
source: Mooney images are black-and-white degraded images that are difficult to recognize at first.
evidence: Description of stimulus properties.

claim: Once the subject is exposed to the original, non-degraded grayscale image, their recognition of the corresponding Mooney image becomes effortless, and this effect can last for days to months, even a lifetime.
source: Yet, once the subject is exposed to the original, non-degraded grayscale image (a process called 'disambiguation'), their recognition of the corresponding Mooney image becomes effortless, and this effect can last for days to months, even a lifetime (Albright, 2012; Ludmer et al., 2011).
evidence: Description of Mooney image phenomenon with citations.

claim: After disambiguation, neural activity patterns elicited by Mooney images in early and category-selective visual regions become more distinct between different images and more similar to those elicited by their matching grayscale counterparts.
source: Recent studies have shown that after disambiguation, neural activity patterns elicited by Mooney images in early and category-selective visual regions become more distinct between different images and more similar to those elicited by their matching grayscale counterparts (Hsieh et al., 2010; Gorlin et al., 2012; van Loon et al., 2016).
evidence: Summary of previous findings with citations.

claim: How prior experience impacts neural processing in higher-order frontoparietal cortices remains largely unknown.
source: However, how prior experience impacts neural processing in higher-order frontoparietal cortices remains largely unknown.
evidence: Statement of knowledge gap.

claim: The study used ultra-high-field (7T) fMRI and multivariate pattern analyses to investigate neural processing of Mooney images before and after disambiguation.
source: In this study, we investigated neural processing of Mooney images before and after disambiguation across the brain, from retinotopic and category-selective visual areas to FPN and DMN, using ultra-high-field (7T) fMRI and multivariate pattern analyses.
evidence: Description of methods used in the study.

claim: The study hypothesized that the acquisition of perceptual priors would alter neural representations and enhance content-specific information in DMN and FPN regions.
source: We hypothesized that the acquisition of perceptual priors would alter neural representations and enhance content-specific information in DMN and FPN regions.
evidence: Statement of hypothesis.

claim: Thirty-three Mooney images were used, 17 of which contained animals, and 16 contained manmade objects.
source: Nineteen subjects were shown 33 Mooney images, 17 of which contained animals, and 16 contained manmade objects.
evidence: Description of experimental stimuli.

claim: Each Mooney image was presented six times before its corresponding gray-scale image was shown to the subject, and six times after.
source: Each Mooney image was presented six times before its corresponding gray-scale image was shown to the subject, and six times after.
evidence: Description of experimental design.

claim: Following each Mooney image presentation, subjects responded to the question 'Can you recognize and name the object in the image?' using a button press.
source: Following each Mooney image presentation, subjects responded to the question 'Can you recognize and name the object in the image?' using a button press ('subjective recognition').
evidence: Description of experimental task.

claim: At the end of each run, Mooney images presented during that run were shown again and participants were asked to verbally report what they saw in the image.
source: To ensure that subjects' self-reported recognition matched the true content of the Mooney images, at the end of each run, Mooney images presented during that run were shown again and participants were asked to verbally report what they saw in the image and were allowed to answer 'unknown'.
evidence: Description of experimental procedure.

claim: Verbal responses were scored as correct or incorrect using a pre-determined list of acceptable responses for each image.
source: Verbal responses were scored as correct or incorrect using a pre-determined list of acceptable responses for each image.
evidence: Description of scoring procedure.

claim: The enhanced image-level information in DMN regions following disambiguation could not be attributed to an overall higher level of signal, since the activity is actually closer to baseline than that elicited by pre-disambiguation Mooney images.
source: Importantly, the enhanced image-level information in DMN regions following disambiguation could not be attributed to an overall higher level of signal, since the activity is actually closer to baseline than that elicited by pre-disambiguation Mooney images.
evidence: Inference from the data showing reduced deactivation rather than increased activation.

claim: DMN regions are actively involved in the processing of visual images during prior-guided perception, as their representation of a given visual stimulus was altered by the presence of a perceptual prior and shifted significantly toward that prior.
source: These results suggest that, even in an externally oriented perceptual task, DMN regions cannot merely encode nonspecific effects such as arousal (Gorlin et al., 2012) or task difficulty (Singh and Fawcett, 2008) as previously postulated. Instead, they are actively involved in the processing of these visual images, as their representation of a given visual stimulus was altered by the presence of a perceptual prior and shifted significantly toward that prior.
evidence: Inference from the data showing content-specific changes in DMN representations.

claim: The profound changes in DMN representations following fast, automatic disambiguation are consistent with a previous finding showing that slow, deliberate perceptual training alters resting-state functional connectivity between DMN regions and the visual cortex.
source: The profound changes in DMN representations following fast, automatic disambiguation uncovered herein resonate with a previous finding showing that slow, deliberate perceptual training alters resting-state functional connectivity between DMN regions and the visual cortex (Lewis et al., 2009).
evidence: Comparison with previous findings with citation.

claim: The results are consistent with a recent study showing greater DMN activation to objects than color patches during a working memory task.
source: Our results are also consistent with a recent study showing greater DMN activation to objects than color patches during a working memory task (Murphy et al., 2018), which, speculatively, may reflect stronger priors for the former learnt through past experiences, although differential stimulus complexity might provide another account for this previous finding.
evidence: Comparison with previous findings with citation and speculation about interpretation.

claim: The FPN exhibited an intermediate pattern compared to DMN and visual areas in prior-guided perceptual processing.
source: Consistent with our prior hypothesis, the FPN exhibited an intermediate pattern compared to DMN and visual areas in this task.
evidence: Summary of findings consistent with hypothesis.

claim: The FPN's neural representational format was intermediate between that of visual areas and DMN.
source: Although all these regions exhibited enhanced image-level information, a higher-dimensional neural representational space, and activity patterns that shifted towards the prior-inducing images following disambiguation, using a second-order RSA, we established that the FPN's neural representational format was indeed intermediate between that of visual areas and DMN.
evidence: Supported by second-order RSA analysis.

claim: The extent to which priors altered neural representations in the FPN was intermediate of that in the visual areas and DMN.
source: In addition, the extent to which priors altered neural representations in the FPN was also intermediate of that in the visual areas and DMN (Figure 7).
evidence: Supported by preservation index analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: All disambiguated Mooney images required the same response (counterbalanced button presses to indicate 'recognized').
source: Because all disambiguated Mooney images required the same response (counterbalanced button presses to indicate 'recognized'), these findings in the FPN do not fit easily with a previous suggestion that the FPN only encode the distinction between targets and non-targets (Erez and Duncan, 2015).
evidence: Description of experimental design and inference about interpretation.

claim: Following disambiguation, frontal areas of the FPN moved up the hierarchy, suggesting that they may have a special role in utilizing priors to guide perceptual processing.
source: Interestingly, although the global hierarchy of neural representation format across cortical areas remained stable across perceptual conditions, following disambiguation frontal areas of the FPN moved up the hierarchy, suggesting that they may have a special role in utilizing priors to guide perceptual processing.
evidence: Inference from the second-order RSA analysis showing changes in hierarchy.

claim: The findings support earlier reports of increased image-level information in early and category-selective visual regions following disambiguation.
source: Outside the DMN and FPN, our findings support earlier reports of increased image-level information in early and category-selective visual regions following disambiguation, as well as a shift of neural representation in visual areas toward the prior-inducing image (Hsieh et al., 2010; Gorlin et al., 2012; van Loon et al., 2016).
evidence: Comparison with previous findings with citations.

claim: Image-specific information increases in V1 following disambiguation.
source: An unresolved issue in these previous studies was whether image-specific information increases in V1 following disambiguation (Gorlin et al., 2012; van Loon et al., 2016); our results suggest that this is indeed the case, in line with the finding in (van Loon et al., 2016).
evidence: Resolution of previous controversy with citation.

claim: FG is consistently placed higher up than LOC along the cortical hierarchy across perceptual conditions.
source: First, FG is consistently placed higher up than LOC along the cortical hierarchy across perceptual conditions (Figure 5); second, FG consistently exhibits higher dimensionality in its neural representational space than LOC across perceptual conditions; last, disambiguation alters neural representation more strongly in FG than LOC.
evidence: Supported by second-order RSA analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: FG consistently exhibits higher dimensionality in its neural representational space than LOC across perceptual conditions.
source: First, FG is consistently placed higher up than LOC along the cortical hierarchy across perceptual conditions (Figure 5); second, FG consistently exhibits higher dimensionality in its neural representational space than LOC across perceptual conditions; last, disambiguation alters neural representation more strongly in FG than LOC.
evidence: Supported by dimensionality analysis.

claim: Disambiguation alters neural representation more strongly in FG than LOC.
source: First, FG is consistently placed higher up than LOC along the cortical hierarchy across perceptual conditions (Figure 5); second, FG consistently exhibits higher dimensionality in its neural representational space than LOC across perceptual conditions; last, disambiguation alters neural representation more strongly in FG than LOC.
evidence: Supported by preservation index analysis.

claim: The results revealing a hierarchy between LOC and FG are compatible with the FG being located more anteriorly than the LOC and previous report of a representational gradient between these two regions.
source: These results revealing a hierarchy between LOC and FG are compatible with the FG being located more anteriorly than the LOC (Figure 2—figure supplement 3) and previous report of a representational gradient between these two regions (Haushofer et al., 2008).
evidence: Inference from anatomical location and comparison with previous findings.

claim: The Mooney image disambiguation effect is a dramatic example of one-shot learning.
source: The Mooney image disambiguation effect is a dramatic example of one-shot learning, where a single exposure to an event leaves a long-term memory in the brain that influences future perception of a different, but related stimulus.
evidence: Characterization of the phenomenon.

claim: The perceptual prior acquired during Mooney image disambiguation differs from episodic memory by being non-self-referential and potentially non-declarative.
source: While the poster child of one-shot memory is episodic memory, the perceptual prior acquired during Mooney image disambiguation differs from episodic memory by being non-self-referential and potentially non-declarative (Ludmer et al., 2011; Chang et al., 2016).
evidence: Characterization of the phenomenon with citations.

claim: A previous study found that activity in mid-level visual regions, MPFC, and amygdala, but not hippocampus, during gray-scale image viewing predicted successful disambiguation of Mooney images.
source: Supporting this distinction, a previous study found that activity in mid-level visual regions, MPFC, and amygdala, but not hippocampus, during gray-scale image viewing predicted successful disambiguation of Mooney images (Ludmer et al., 2011).
evidence: Summary of previous findings with citation.

claim: The study did not find a significant increase in image-specific information following disambiguation in anatomically defined hippocampal ROIs.
source: In accordance, we did not find a significant increase in image-specific information following disambiguation in anatomically defined hippocampal ROIs.
evidence: Negative finding from the current study.

claim: If prior experiences overwhelm sensory input, hallucinations may follow, as happens in post-traumatic stress disorder.
source: For instance, if prior experiences overwhelm sensory input, hallucinations may follow, as happens in post-traumatic stress disorder (Clancy et al., 2017).
evidence: Clinical implication with citation.

claim: Psychosis-prone individuals have a larger disambiguation effect than control subjects in the Mooney image paradigm.
source: Similarly, psychosis-prone individuals have a larger disambiguation effect than control subjects in the Mooney image paradigm, consistent with the idea that internal priors play an especially strong role in shaping perception during psychosis (Teufel et al., 2015).
evidence: Summary of previous findings with citation.

claim: Prior experience impacts visual perceptual processing throughout the cortical hierarchy, from occipitotemporal visual regions to frontoparietal and default-mode networks.
source: In conclusion, we observed that prior experience impacts visual perceptual processing throughout the cortical hierarchy, from occipitotemporal visual regions to frontoparietal and default-mode networks.
evidence: Summary of main findings.

claim: There is a macroscale hierarchy of neural representation format, with increased dimensionality in neural representational space and more profound influences of perceptual prior on neural representations in higher-order frontoparietal regions.
source: In addition, we observed a macroscale hierarchy of neural representation format, with increased dimensionality in neural representational space and more profound influences of perceptual prior on neural representations in higher-order frontoparietal regions.
evidence: Summary of main findings.

claim: The results reveal content-specific neural representations in frontoparietal and default-mode networks involved in prior-guided visual perception.
source: These results reveal content-specific neural representations in frontoparietal and default-mode networks involved in prior-guided visual perception.
evidence: Summary of main conclusion.

claim: All participants were right-handed and neurologically healthy, with normal or corrected-to-normal vision.
source: All participants were right-handed and neurologically healthy, with normal or corrected-to-normal vision.
evidence: Description of participant characteristics.

claim: The experiment was approved by the Institutional Review Board of the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke.
source: The experiment was approved by the Institutional Review Board of the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke.
evidence: Statement of ethical approval.

claim: All subjects provided written informed consent.
source: All subjects provided written informed consent.
evidence: Statement of ethical procedure.

claim: Mooney and gray-scale images were generated from gray-scale photographs of real-world man-made objects and animals selected from the Caltech and Pascal VOC databases.
source: Briefly, Mooney and gray-scale images were generated from gray-scale photographs of real-world man-made objects and animals selected from the Caltech (http://www.vision.caltech.edu/Image_Datasets/Caltech101/Caltech101.html) and Pascal VOC (http://host.robots.ox.ac.uk/pascal/VOC/voc2012/index.html) databases.
evidence: Description of stimulus generation procedure.

claim: Images with the largest disambiguation effect were chosen for the study based on an initial screening procedure performed by six additional subjects.
source: Out of an original set of 252 images, 33 (16 were man-made objects, the rest animals – unbeknownst to the subjects) were chosen for the experiment via an initial screening procedure, which was performed by six additional subjects recruited separately from the main experiment. Images with the largest disambiguation effect – assessed by changes in difficulty rating before vs. after disambiguation – were chosen for this study.
evidence: Description of stimulus selection procedure.

claim: Images were projected onto a screen located at the back of the scanner and subtended approximately 11.9 × 11.9 degrees of visual angle.
source: Images were projected onto a screen located at the back of the scanner and subtended approximately 11.9 × 11.9 degrees of visual angle.
evidence: Description of stimulus presentation parameters.

claim: Imaging was performed on a Siemens 7T MRI scanner equipped with a 32-channel head coil.
source: Imaging was performed on a Siemens 7T MRI scanner equipped with a 32-channel head coil (Nova Medical, Wilmington, MA, USA).
evidence: Description of imaging equipment.

claim: T1-weighted anatomical images were obtained using a magnetization-prepared rapid-acquisition gradient echo (MP-RAGE) sequence with 1 × 1×1 mm resolution.
source: T1-weighted anatomical images were obtained using a magnetization-prepared rapid-acquisition gradient echo (MP-RAGE) sequence (sagittal orientation, 1 × 1×1 mm resolution).
evidence: Description of imaging parameters.

claim: Functional images were obtained using a single-shot echo planar imaging (EPI) sequence with TR = 2000 ms, TE = 25 ms, flip angle = 50°, 52 oblique slices, slice thickness = 2 mm, spacing = 0 mm, in-plane resolution = 1.8×1.8 mm.
source: Functional images were obtained using a single-shot echo planar imaging (EPI) sequence (TR = 2000 ms, TE = 25 ms, flip angle = 50°, 52 oblique slices, slice thickness = 2 mm, spacing = 0 mm, in-plane resolution = 1.8×1.8 mm, FOV = 192 mm, acceleration factor/GRAPPA = 3).
evidence: Description of imaging parameters.

claim: Respiration and cardiac data were collected using a breathing belt and a pulse oximeter.
source: Respiration and cardiac data were collected using a breathing belt and a pulse oximeter, respectively. The breathing belt was wrapped around the upper abdomen, and the pulse oximeter was placed around the left index finger.
evidence: Description of physiological data collection.

claim: Physiological noise was removed from functional data using the RETROICOR method.
source: Functional data preprocessing started with the removal of physiological (respiration- and cardiac-related) noise using the RETROICOR method (Glover et al., 2000).
evidence: Description of preprocessing method with citation.
